canonicalExplanation.summary: `git merge feature` brings feature's work into the current branch. Git first finds the **merge base**, the last commit both share. If main hasn't moved since then, it's a **fast-forward**: main's pointer simply slides up to feature's tip, and no new commit is made. If both sides have new commits, it's a **three-way merge**: Git combines base, main and feature into a new **merge commit** with two parents. No conflicts only means **no overlapping text edits**. The result can still be broken, so **run the tests after every merge**.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner merges their feature into main and is surprised that `git log` shows no merge commit. A week later a teammate's merge creates one. Which is right? When main has not advanced, merging feature fast-forwards main to the feature commit without creating an extra merge commit. In this lesson you'll perform and explain fast-forward and divergent merges in a disposable repository.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Commits and history** (commits and their parents) and **Short-lived feature branches** (starting from a fresh base).

sections.heading: The model: fast-forward vs three-way
sections.body:
```text
fast-forward (main hasn't moved):
  A --- B (main)             A --- B --- C --- D (main, feature)
         \          ==>
          C --- D (feature)

three-way (both moved):
  A --- B --- E (main)       A --- B --- E --- M (main)
         \          ==>             \         /
          C --- D (feature)          C --- D (feature)
```

```bash
git switch main
git merge-base main feature    # the shared commit B.
git merge feature              # "Fast-forward", or a merge commit M.
git log --oneline --graph      # see the shape.
npm test                       # verify the combined behaviour.
# Optional: git merge --no-ff feature always records a merge commit.
```

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why might a team use --no-ff?", "answer": "It always records a merge commit, keeping a visible marker of where the feature started and ended, even when a fast-forward was possible."}
```

sections.heading: Clean isn't correct

includes: Explain the merge base, fast-forward merges and three-way merge commits.
Verify merged behaviour with tests, since a conflict-free merge can still be wrong.

outcomes: Perform and explain fast-forward and divergent merges in a disposable repository.

examples.title: Main hasn't moved
examples.situation: When main has not advanced, merging feature fast-forwards main to the feature commit without creating an extra merge commit.
walkthrough: **Main has not advanced:** git merge-base main feature equals main's tip.
**Fast-forwards main to the feature commit:** git merge feature prints "Fast-forward" and main now points at D.
**Without creating an extra merge commit:** git log --graph will show a straight line; tests still run afterwards.
examples.result: The learner knows why no merge commit appeared, and that it's correct.

examples.title: The divergent merge
examples.situation: While feature was in review, main gained a hotfix commit E. Now both branches have new work.
walkthrough: merge-base is B, older than both tips.
git merge feature creates merge commit M with parents E and D.
Tests run on M, because this exact combination never existed before.
examples.result: Both lines of work are combined, and the combination is verified.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A merge is successful and correct whenever Git reports no textual conflicts.
misconceptions.correction: Git only checks whether the same lines were edited. Changes in different places can still contradict each other, so behaviour must be tested after merging.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "Clean isn't correct", why did the app fail?

analogy.example: Fast-forward is like **catching up on a TV series nobody else touched**: you just jump to the latest episode. A three-way merge is **two writers each continuing the story from episode 5**: an editor combines both into a new episode 7. Even if their pages don't overlap, the plots can still contradict each other.
limitations: Git's editor only compares lines, not meaning.
Tests are the reader who notices the plot hole.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable repo, create a feature branch with two commits and merge it into an unchanged main. Then repeat with a commit on main first. Show both graphs and name each merge type.

farTransfer.prompt: Build the rename example: on one branch rename a function, on another add a new call using the old name. Merge without conflicts, show that a test fails, then fix it in a follow-up commit and explain why Git couldn't detect the problem.
scaffold: Edit different lines so no conflict appears.
A tiny test script is enough.

remediation.explanation: Before merging: **what's the merge base, and has main moved?** After merging: **run the tests**, whatever Git reported.

recap.summary: To perform and explain merges, find the merge base, expect a fast-forward pointer move when the target hasn't advanced and a two-parent merge commit when both sides moved, and always test the merged result, because a conflict-free merge can still combine into broken behaviour.
